notes.claim: UK domestic supply is nominally 230 V, 50 Hz, kept within 216 V to 253 V by the Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations.
Ships mostly run 60 Hz, because higher frequency lets motors and generators run faster and so be smaller for a given power.
A single coil turned at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field produces an emf that varies sinusoidally in time.
The induced emf depends on how quickly the flux through the coil is changing, so a faster-turning coil gives a larger voltage.
For i1: a real a.c. generator holds its terminal voltage by adjusting its d.c. field current (screen 12's Why? and the explain).
The rms value of an AC quantity is the DC that would produce the same heating in the same resistance.
For a sine wave the rms value is approximately 0.707 of the peak, which is the reciprocal of the square root of 2.
UK mains is 230 V rms, so its peak is about 325 V (230 times root 2), according to one school revision site; the nominal 230 V itself is set by ESQCR.
For i2: an analogue meter's needle follows the average of the AC, and its rms calibration assumes a sine wave (screens 9, 10 and 12, the explain and practice).
For i2: appliances and devices are quoted with rms values rather than peak values (the explain and the practice's first bullet).
For i2: most ships run a 440 V system, so as an example its peak is 440 x root 2 = 622 V (computed; SECONDARY; screen 8's Why? and the explain).
In a resistor, voltage and current are in phase: both curves reach maxima and minima together.
The product of rms voltage and rms current in a resistor equals the average power.
The instantaneous power in a resistor oscillates at twice the frequency of the voltage and never goes negative.
In a pure inductor the voltage leads the current, that is, the current lags behind the voltage.
Inductive reactance is X_L = 2πfL, in ohms, and is directly proportional to the frequency of the alternating current.
A capacitor opposes changes in voltage by drawing or supplying current as it charges or discharges to the new voltage level.
In a capacitor the current leads the voltage, so the voltage lags behind the current.
Capacitive reactance is X_C = 1/(2πfC) and decreases as frequency rises, the opposite of inductive reactance.
The phasors for a resistor and a reactance are 90 degrees apart, so the series impedance comes from Pythagoras' law.
Voltages 90 degrees apart do not add arithmetically: a 6 V source and an 8 V source at 90 degrees give 10 V.
Inductive reactance is X_L = 2πfL, so a measured reactance at a known frequency gives the inductance.
In a series RLC circuit the current is greatest at the resonant frequency, where impedance is minimum and X_L equals X_C.
At resonance the voltage across L or C in a series circuit is Q times the applied voltage, which can be dangerously high.
Capacitors and inductors absorb energy during one half-cycle and return it in the other, so the power wave goes below zero.
True power is measured in watts, reactive power in volt-amps reactive (VAR), and their combination is apparent power in volt-amps.
Power factor is true power divided by apparent power, which equals the cosine of the phase angle; average power is V I cos φ with rms values.
Any power factor less than 1 means the wiring must carry more current to deliver the same true power.
A poor power factor can be corrected by adding a load drawing equal and opposite reactive power, which means a capacitor for an inductive load.
Correction does not change the true power consumed, but cuts apparent power and the total current drawn from the source.
Too much capacitance gives a low power factor just as too much inductance does, so a correction must not over-correct.
A three-phase generator has three coils of wire placed at 120 degrees to each other and rotated in a magnetic field.
The line voltage is found by taking the phasor sum of the voltages in two phases, which gives the factor root 3.
In balanced star circuits line voltage is root 3 times phase voltage and line current equals phase current; in balanced delta the roles reverse.
Three-phase power equals the product of line-to-line voltage, line current, root 3 and the power factor.
The neutral conductor carries no current in a balanced three-phase network.
Triplen harmonic currents add within the neutral of a 4-wire Y-Y system, so 'balanced means no neutral current' holds for sine-wave loads.
